Paternity means the state or fact of being a father — specifically, the relationship that exists between a father and his child.

Just as the word "motherhood" describes what it means to be a mother, paternity describes what it means to be a father — the role, the responsibility, and the bond that comes with it.

Paternity has two closely linked dimensions:

  1. Biological paternity — the genetic/blood connection between a man and his child. If a man is the biological father of a child, that is his biological paternity.
  2. Legal paternity — the official, recognized status of a man as a child's father in the eyes of the law. This matters because it determines rights (like spending time with the child) and responsibilities (like financially supporting the child).

These two don't always perfectly overlap. A man can be a child's biological father without being the legal father, and vice versa (for example, in adoption).
Why Paternity Matters in Real Life

Paternity is significant in several important practical situations:

When a couple is not married, the father's identity is not automatically assumed by law the way it often is within a marriage. Paternity may need to be formally established — either both parents sign a document acknowledging it, or a court decides it.

In disputes — if there is disagreement or uncertainty about who fathered a child, the matter may go to court. This is called a paternity case or paternity suit. Courts use this process to legally determine who the father is.

For inheritance and benefits — a child may need legally confirmed paternity to inherit from their father, to claim financial support, or to access certain legal rights.

You will very commonly see the phrase paternity test. This is a DNA test used to determine, with near-certainty, whether a specific man is the biological father of a specific child. DNA from both the man and the child is compared; if they share the right genetic patterns, paternity is confirmed.

Paternity tests are used in legal cases, in personal situations where there is genuine uncertainty, or simply for peace of mind.

Another very common use: paternity leave refers to the period of time off from work that a new father is given (or entitled to, in many countries) after the birth or adoption of a child. It is the father's equivalent of maternity leave (which is taken by the mother).

Less commonly, "paternity" is used in a figurative sense to mean the origin or authorship of something — like an idea, a work of art, or an invention. For example: "The paternity of this theory is disputed — no one is sure who first proposed it." Here, the word is used metaphorically, treating the creator of something the way we'd treat the father of a child.

This usage is relatively rare and mostly appears in formal or literary writing.

The adjective form of this word is paternal, meaning "relating to a father" — for example, paternal love, paternal instinct, or paternal grandfather (your father's father). Knowing this helps you recognize the whole family of words built on the same idea.
